one_liner: Archived C99 port of Bob Jenkins' SpookyV2 128-bit hash; about 11-20% faster than xxHash64 on large keys.
what_it_does: A plain-C packaging of SpookyV2, Bob Jenkins' 2012 non-cryptographic hash. It takes any byte array and a 128-bit seed and returns a 128-bit value; the 64- and 32-bit variants just keep the low bits. The API has one-shot spookyhash_128/_64/_32 calls and a streaming spookyhash_context (init/update/final), with all state held in the caller's struct rather than a C++ object. It is not a drop-in for XXH64: the function names and seed conventions differ, and so do the hash values.
how_it_is_fast: Inputs of 192 bytes or more go through a 'trickle-feed' Mix over 12 64-bit state variables in 96-byte blocks. Each 8-byte word is added to one variable, followed by a few xor/rotate/add steps, so the 12 independent lanes give the CPU a lot of instruction-level parallelism with only add, xor and rotate: no SIMD and no multiplies. Jenkins reports that SSE2 and 64-bit multiply variants were slower. Inputs under 192 bytes take a separate 4-variable ShortHash, and a cheaper End() (three end_partial rounds) finishes long inputs.
when_to_use: Checksumming large, cache-resident buffers (roughly 1 KB and up) on 64-bit CPUs without depending on SIMD or AES: SpookyV2_64 averaged 13,401 MiB/s against 11,177 MiB/s for xxHash64 on 256 KB keys in rurban/smhasher.
You need 128-bit output from plain C with no platform-specific instructions, for example content fingerprints or dedup keys where 64-bit collision odds are too high.

You must reproduce existing SpookyV2 values from C code, such as stored keys or Bloom filters built with SpookyV2. The port's self-test uses the same 512 expected Hash32 values as Bob Jenkins' TestSpookyV2.cpp.
Data arrives in fragments and you want a streaming context whose result matches the one-shot hash. The port's test_pieces checks every two-piece split of inputs up to 1 KB.
You want a seeded 32-bit hash that passes the full SMHasher3 battery: SpookyHash2-32 is listed as passing 250 of 250 tests.
when_not_to_use: Short keys such as hash-table lookups on 32 bytes or less: it averages 56.2 cycles/hash against 49.7 for xxHash64 in rurban/smhasher (60.2 vs 52.6 in SMHasher3). At 16-31 bytes it rises to about 66-71 cycles.

New code that doesn't need SpookyV2-compatible values. XXH3, wyhash and rapidhash beat it on both bulk and small keys; in rurban/smhasher they reach 20,854, 22,641 and 21,514 MiB/s, and rapidhash takes about 22 cycles/hash.
Untrusted or adversarial input, where hash flooding is a risk. It is non-cryptographic, and Jenkins' page says a resourceful opponent can build colliding messages.

Big-endian targets. Open issue #17 (2022) reports wrong results on s390x because the short-input tail reads skip the byte swap. The self-test only prints mismatches and always exits 0, so the QEMU PowerPC CI never caught it, and the archived repo will not get a fix.

Streaming data from RAM rather than cache. Jenkins notes that uncached memory reads cap it below about 2 bytes/cycle on his machines, so the bulk lead measured on cache-resident 256 KB keys may disappear.

integration.form: source-drop (three .c files; premake5 can also build static and shared libraries)
integration.dependencies: none (C standard headers only). premake5 is needed only for the bundled build, and the cputime git submodule only for the test binary.
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (premake sets cdialect C99). The now-defunct Travis/AppVeyor CI covered GCC 4.8-7, Clang 3.5-5.0, MSVC 2015 and MinGW.
integration.platforms: Little-endian 32- or 64-bit CPUs (CI covered x86, x64, ARM and aarch64, the latter two under QEMU). Big-endian builds compile but give wrong results for some short inputs (issue #17).
integration.thread_safety: Reentrant: there is no global state, so one-shot calls can run concurrently. Each thread needs its own spookyhash_context (README: 'multithreading via context variables').

gotchas: spookyhash_api.h closes its extern "C" block right after the version functions. The hash and context functions therefore get C++ linkage when included from C++, which causes undefined references against the C-compiled library, so wrap the #include in extern "C" { } yourself.
spookyhash_128's hash_1/hash_2 pointers are in-out: they carry the seed in and the hash out. Reusing the same variables across calls silently chains seeds.

Unaligned reads are off by default (SPOOKYHASH_ALLOW_UNALIGNED_READS 0), so misaligned input is memcpy'd per 96-byte block, or whole for inputs under 192 bytes. The reference SpookyV2.cpp used in the SMHasher runs reads unaligned directly, so this port's speed on misaligned input is unmeasured.

Don't treat the 128-bit output's two halves as independent for short keys. SMHasher3 fails SpookyHash2-128 on BIC for 3-28-byte keys (235/250 passed), while the 64-bit output fails only 6 seed-sensitivity tests on 3-11-byte keys.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over XXH3, wyhash or rapidhash only when you need SpookyV2-compatible values or a portable 128-bit result without SIMD, since all three beat it on bulk and small-key speed. Against pengyhash, which matches it on rurban bulk throughput (13,347 vs 13,401 MiB/s), it fails fewer SMHasher3 tests (6 vs 16) and has higher bulk throughput there (4.40 vs 3.80 bytes/cycle).
verified_claims_summary: In rurban/smhasher's bulk test (262,144-byte cache-resident keys, averaged over alignments 0-7, on the reference AMD Ryzen 5 3350G, with MiB/s derived from bytes/cycle at a nominal 3 GHz), Bob Jenkins' C++ SpookyV2_64 averaged 13,401 MiB/s against 11,177 for xxHash64, about 20% faster. SMHasher3 shows 14.40 vs 13.02 GiB/s (about 11%; its results page does not state the hardware). Neither suite states compiler or flags, both measured the reference C++ code rather than this C port, and xxHash64 wins on keys of 32 bytes or less in both.
status_note: Archived and read-only: the last code change was v1.0.7 in January 2018 (the 2021 commit only removed org references) and issue #17's big-endian bug is unfixed, but it is BSD-3-Clause and three .c files are easy to vendor. For new code the better upstream is Bob Jenkins' own reference, published in March 2026 at github.com/bobjen/spookyhash (C++ plus a Rust translation, Unlicense).
